featured.name: Pixel3D
featured.summary: A look-development sandbox for low-poly worlds with pixel palettes, lighting, weather, and stacked screen effects.
featured.outcome: One look-development toolkit now drives three very different scenes, and its presets became the visual base for a later game prototype.
featured.problem: How far can a real-time 3D scene be pushed toward a hand-made pixel-art look?
featured.built: Three explorable scenes — a forest, a woodland kingdom, and a Japanese school — plus an overlay editor for palettes, ordered effect stacks, vegetation, shadows, weather, undo/redo, and saved looks.
featured.flavor: Three small worlds, and one lantern to see them all by.
featured.note: Rendering work adapts supplied compositor effects alongside original environment and interaction work. These are studies, not released games.

projects.name: Bonfire Portfolio
projects.summary: The site you’re on: a 3D bonfire drawn as pixel art that burns behind every page, forges a new weapon for each project you open, and can be taken apart to show how it’s made.
projects.problem: Portfolios tend to read like résumés. I wanted mine to play like the games I make, without slowing down someone who only wants to skim the projects.
projects.built: A Three.js scene drawn small in three passes (normals, lit color, glowing particles) and finished by one pixel pass that outlines, dithers and snaps every pixel to the flame’s palette. The fire is particles carried by a curl-noise flow field. Opening a project forges one of 23 Blender-modeled weapons in fire, lightning or ice; a pack swaps between five places to burn, the weapons and spells; and a knight in steel plate answers a summon sign glowing on the ground, forming out of it in the fire’s element, resting a while and burning away again, drawn in a hand-drawn pixel-art style the pack can change. Around it: photo mode, discoveries, a title, description and social image for every page, and an admin whose live preview shows every effect before it commits the change to GitHub. Bonfire Live and its scene editor, the Bonfire Painter, run on the same engine.
projects.flavor: Every fire can be taken apart. This one wants to be.
projects.note: Works by keyboard throughout. Phones get fewer particles and no shadows; reduced motion gets a calmer fire and instant camera cuts.

projects.name: Bonfire Live
projects.summary: This site’s bonfire turned into a live visualizer for DJ sets: it hears the beat, the build-ups and the drops, and answers with fire, lightning and ice.
projects.outcome: Runs a live show from one laptop: it locks to the DJ’s beat by ear or through Ableton Link, and plays full screen on a projector.
projects.problem: Most visualizers only follow loudness, so a build-up and a drop look alike and nothing on screen feels like it’s performing with the DJ.
projects.built: A browser visualizer on the portfolio’s pixel-art renderer: beat and tempo tracking, section detection that forges a new weapon in the breakdown and strikes it on the drop, a living blade that fights on the beat with cinematic follow cameras, rave looks (kaleidoscope, mirrors, echo, glitch) and palettes generated on the fly. Up to four knights rest by the fire in any of the knight’s styles and get up to dance on the drop (the Default Dance among their moves), and a Render tab sets how the picture is drawn: pixel size, palette, dither, outlines, fog and x-ray views of its passes. Preset Scenes, painted in the Bonfire Painter, set all of it at once (the place, the colors, the framing and its move, the look, the knights, the render), and the show loops through them, each arriving in a drop’s flash or on a phrase line.
projects.flavor: The fire dances when the music is right.
projects.note: Runs in a desktop browser on line-in, tab audio, an audio file or the built-in demo track.

projects.name: Bonfire Painter
projects.summary: A scene editor for Bonfire Live: paint the place, the fire’s colors, the camera and its slow move, a look and its layers, the knights and the render, watch it play to a silent beat, then send it to Bonfire Live, which loops through scenes like it.
projects.problem: Bonfire Live rolls its own looks, colors and camera shots as the music plays. There was no way to set up a whole scene by hand, keep it, and have the show come back to it.
projects.built: A page on Bonfire Live’s own engine and director, holding the scene through the same scene player, so what’s painted is what plays. A panel in ten folding sections reaches every part of a scene: the place, the weapon and element, the flame’s and the scenery’s colors, the camera (orbit it on the stage, or start from one of the show’s shots), the ten looks and their details, the layers, the drops, the render, the knights (style, finish, seat pose, the Default Dance) and the fireflies. Hovering a flame, a look, a shot or a layer shows it on the stage at once; every detail can be pinned or left to the dice, rolled again each time the look comes round. It previews in Still, a silent 124 BPM beat, a silent 16-bar drop loop or the demo track, with undo, a draft that autosaves, and a library of saved scenes with thumbnails, JSON import and export. Play in Bonfire Live hands the scene to an open Bonfire Live tab, or opens one playing it. Bonfire Live’s four built-in scenes were painted here.
projects.flavor: The fire can be painted too.
projects.note: Every field has a “?” that says what it does. On a phone the panel becomes a bottom sheet with a strip of section tabs; with reduced motion it opens on the Still preview. Saved scenes stay in this browser, and Export makes a file of them.

projects.name: Gamex
projects.summary: A TypeScript 2D engine with a browser studio where scenes, sprites, UI, and effects are built in one place.
projects.outcome: Proven by building a real game in it: the Reliquary of Ash browser prototype.
projects.problem: Making a game means jumping between separate tools for assets, scenes, behavior, and UI.
projects.built: A 2D engine and browser-based studio with scene, sprite, and UI editors, WebGL2 effects, a shared command API, and an embedded AI agent — tested by building a real game in it.
projects.flavor: A forge for small worlds. Every tool it holds was made to build the next.
projects.note: Private repository — case study and captures only. Alpha software; usability hasn’t been measured with outside users yet.

paragraphs: I’m Newton, a Seattle developer who came to code the long way — through digital media arts, graphic design, and managing a busy tea shop. Today I build full-stack internal platforms at Lyft, and in my own time I build game engines, prototypes, and pixel-art worlds.
I like tools that get out of the way and games that pull you in. Both come down to understanding the person on the other side of the screen.
Away from the keyboard, I lead youth programs in my community and tinker with tabletop game design.

bullets: Build full-stack internal platforms for the Connected Experience team, used in employee workflows across the company.
Create Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that bring AI tools into everyday employee work.

roles.title: IT Support Intern
bullets: Contributed front-end and full-stack work to more than four internal software projects.
Supported Mac and PC users, networks, device provisioning, and onboarding; wrote troubleshooting guides and procedures.
Ran daily IT Support stand-ups and joined biweekly sprint planning and retros.

items.text: Led six mentors and built curriculum for ages 14–17. Organized two volunteer events that raised $10,000 for nonprofits.
Supervised a 12-person team serving up to 400 guests at peak, and helped open a new location.
Ran scheduling, onboarding, and daily operations for a team of 10–12.
Led a creative team producing an outreach animation for the Bellevue Stream Team.
Pitched and produced a bilingual English/Spanish health campaign in Adobe Creative Suite.
